findings.source_passage: Among sea-commanders, the old greybeards will oftenest leave their berths to visit the night-cloaked deck.
findings.source_locator: paragraph 2, between 'Old age is always wakeful' and 'It was so with Ahab'
findings.why_it_matters: This sentence carries the generalizing, essayistic rhythm that defines Melville's narrative voice in this chapter; its excision collapses the transition from universal observation to Ahab-specific application, flattening the rhetorical movement.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the sentence between 'Old age is always wakeful' and 'It was so with Ahab' to preserve the characteristic move from general maxim to particular instance.

findings.source_passage: Some considering touch of humanity was in him; for at times like these, he usually abstained from patrolling the quarter-deck
findings.why_it_matters: The phrase 'Some considering touch of humanity was in him' is interpretively loaded—it is one of the few moments the narrator grants Ahab an unqualified humane quality; flattening it to 'usually abstained' strips that moral complexity.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'Some considering touch of humanity was in him' verbatim before the abstaining clause.

findings.source_passage: Stubb, thou didst not know Ahab then. 'Am I a cannon-ball, Stubb,'
findings.source_locator: paragraph 3, transition between Stubb's suggestion and Ahab's reply
findings.why_it_matters: The narratorial aside 'Ah! Stubb, thou didst not know Ahab then' is a famous, tone-establishing interjection that foreshadows the full horror of Ahab's character; its absence removes the narrator's direct address and prophetic coloring.
findings.suggested_fix: Insert 'Ah! Stubb, thou didst not know Ahab then.' as a stand-alone sentence before Ahab's reply to preserve the narrator's ominous aside.

findings.source_passage: It's worth a fellow's while to be born into the world, if only to fall right asleep. And now that I think of it, that's about the first thing babies do, and that's a sort of queer, too. Damn me, but all things are queer, come to think of 'em. But that's against my principles.
findings.source_locator: Stubb's soliloquy, after 'Here goes for a snooze'
findings.why_it_matters: This passage is the comic heart of Stubb's soliloquy—his bathetic philosophy of sleep and babies is both character-defining and a voice-establishing moment of dramatic irony; omitting it guts Stubb's characterization and the chapter's tonal counterweight to Ahab's menace.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore Stubb's reflection on babies, sleep, and his twelfth commandment context ('Damn me, it's worth a fellow's while…But that's against my principles') before the return to Ahab's insults.

findings.source_passage: How's that?—didn't he call me a dog? blazes! he called me ten times a donkey, and piled a lot of jackasses on top of that!
findings.why_it_matters: The exclamation 'blazes!' and 'piled a lot of jackasses on top of that!' carry Stubb's comic indignation; the draft's compression ('pile jackasses on top of that') softens the exclamatory rhythm slightly.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'blazes!' and the fuller phrasing for fidelity to Stubb's voice register.

findings.source_passage: I was never served so before without giving a hard blow for it,
source_locator": "between Stubb's retreat and his extended soliloquy
findings.why_it_matters: This line establishes that Stubb is genuinely shaken—it is his first interior reaction and frames the entire soliloquy that follows; its absence makes the soliloquy begin abruptly.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the short 'I was never served so before without giving a hard blow for it' as the opening of Stubb's belowdecks reflection.

summary: The draft preserves most dialogue and some notable prose but drops or flattens four medium-weight passages—the generalizing sea-commanders sentence, the 'considering touch of humanity' moral note, the narrator's 'Ah! Stubb, thou didst not know Ahab then' aside, and Stubb's comic baby/sleep/eleventh-commandment soliloquy—collectively erasing the chapter's rhetorical architecture and Stubb's defining comic voice.
